body: Puerto Rico is a United States overseas territory, so it counts as the US for country streaks.
The Generation 3 car has an antenna on the front right with a white dot on top, similar to Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands.
Puerto Rico also has smallcam coverage, a low-camera variant of Generation 4 with a wide blur and often a visible antenna.
The primary area code for all of Puerto Rico is (787), with (939) also in use but less common.
Spanish is commonly seen on signs throughout Puerto Rico, often instead of English.
American store chains like Wal-Mart are very common, helping distinguish it from other Latin American countries.
Front plates are not required, which helps differentiate Puerto Rico from Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands where they are mandatory.
A large portion of rural coverage is on large divided highways.
Puerto Rico has unique highway shields for its primary, urban, secondary, and tertiary roads that are not found in any other US state or territory.
Speed limit signs are identical to those in the mainland US but are always in Spanish.
Stop signs say "PARE", which is also used throughout South America and the Dominican Republic.
Kilometre markers are tall and green, with "km" at the top and the number written vertically.
Most homes are made of concrete with flat roofs, and often have metal gates in front.
Official coverage is mostly around major cities like San Juan and Ponce, and in coastal areas.
The southern part of Puerto Rico often has a distinctly drier climate and appearance.
The north and south coasts typically feature flat coastal plains or rolling hills.
The central part of the island is mountainous, with most coverage limited to divided highways.
The southern city of Ponce features unique Ponce Creole architecture, a mix of Victorian and Spanish Revival styles.
Old Town San Juan has narrow streets, colourful buildings with mixed European architecture, and some streets paved with blue cobblestones.
